title: Hey, states: You can just do things
author: Michael J. Petrilli
summary: Michael Petrilli argues that states should follow the Southern Surge playbook of Mississippi and others by acting directly on curriculum, reading instruction, coaching and teacher preparation instead of nudging districts. He recounts how Mississippi, under state superintendent Carey Wright, used every lever from hiring coaches to pressing ed schools and leaning on local curriculum decisions. He asks why the model has not spread and finds that most state science-of-reading laws are half measures. Resistance comes from unions invoking professional autonomy in blue states and from the older tight-loose framing in red states. Petrilli admits his own long advocacy of tight-loose and wonders whether the Southern states found a better way. He names two risks, states getting it wrong and demoralizing professionals, and prescribes safeguards: focus on strong evidence, allow local variation, offer waivers and escape hatches, and collect frontline feedback.
points: The Mississippi model worked because the state acted as if it ran the schools, directly hiring coaches, designing professional learning and pressing teacher preparation toward change.
Most state science-of-reading laws are half measures, such as publishing long lists of approved materials without requiring districts to use them.
Petrilli questions the tight-loose doctrine he once championed, suggesting that evaluating results while leaving methods to districts may be a bank-shot strategy.
The two main risks of state mandates are bad guidance spreading statewide and demoralizing professionals who feel stripped of decision-making authority.
His safeguards are evidence-focused mandates, room for local variation, waiver policies, carve-outs for schools of choice, and honest feedback channels from teachers.
quotes: For decades, many of us in education policy (and ed reform) thought these topics were taboo for state lawmakers and state ed department bureaucrats, thanks to America’s well-entrenched tradition of local control. Then a few (mostly Southern) states decided otherwise.

She didn’t respect the timid traditional role of states versus districts—for example, just providing small grants to a few local education agencies to pilot stronger approaches to teaching reading, or merely using her bully pulpit to encourage local educators to do the right thing. No, she acted like she ran the schools and used every lever she could find to push a coherent vision of teaching and learning (especially around early reading) from the state capital to the classroom.
But most are half measures. Maybe they require the state to publish a list of high-quality instructional materials, but they don’t make local districts use those materials.

In blue states, pushback often comes from (where else?) the teachers unions under the banner of “professional autonomy.” That is mostly (yet another) indication of who has power within the unions—the older, more senior teachers who don’t want states restricting their instructional practices, versus the newer teachers who would benefit the most from clear guidance.
It’s akin to the autonomy-in-return-for-accountability bargain at the heart of charter schooling. States should evaluate the finished meal, so to speak, not dictate the recipe or cooking methods.

First, states might get it wrong. In the long history of American education, countless fads and fashions have whipped through our field, and state education agencies and their leaders have hardly been immune.

Second, people don’t like being bossed around, especially those who call themselves professionals and those engaged in knowledge work. Stripping frontline staff of decision-making authority can demoralize and alienate them.

States would also be smart to allow for real escape hatches—waiver policies that let schools or districts opt out, carve-outs for schools of choice, plus mechanisms to get honest feedback from frontline educators about how it’s going.
